title: Supreme Court Removes Government Supervision Over Kerala Waqf Board
excerpt: The apex court deleted the Kerala High Court's direction placing the Waqf Board under a Joint Secretary's administration, though restrictions on major decisions remain amid an ongoing challenge to the Board's composition.
body:
• The Supreme Court deleted the Kerala High Court's direction that placed the Kerala Waqf Board under the supervision of a state government Joint Secretary.
  • The HC had on July 15 restrained the Board from major decisions after finding it lacked the two non-Muslim members mandated by the 2025 Waqf Amendment Act.
  • The Board appealed to the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear the matter urgently and removed the supervision clause while the composition challenge continues.
  • A Shia group has separately moved the High Court seeking representation on the Board, adding another dimension to the reconstitution dispute.

SC Intervenes in Kerala Waqf Board Standoff

The Supreme Court on Monday deleted a Kerala High Court direction that had placed the Kerala State Waqf Board under the administration and supervision of a Joint Secretary in the state government, according to Bar and Bench and Live Law. The ruling came after the Board filed an urgent appeal against the High Court's sweeping July 15 interim order, which had also barred it from taking major decisions, incurring capital expenditure, or making policy decisions without the court's express permission.

Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, along with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana, heard the appeal after the matter was listed on an urgent basis. The Bench removed the part of the High Court order that required the Board to function under a government official's oversight, while allowing the broader composition challenge to proceed before the High Court.

What the Kerala High Court Had Ordered

On July 15, a Division Bench of Kerala High Court Chief Justice Soumen Sen and Justice Syam Kumar V.M. passed the interim order after hearing four public interest litigations challenging the Board's constitution. The petitioners — BJP state vice president Shone George, a Christian trust named Assembly of Christian Trust Services (ACTS), and retired Army officer Stalin V.M. — argued that the Board was functioning illegally without the two non-Muslim members mandated under Section 14 of the Unified Waqf Management, Empowerment, Efficiency and Development (UMEED) Act, 1995, as amended in 2025.

"Two non-Muslim members have not been included in the Waqf Board... we hold that the constitution of the Board prima facie appears to be not in conformity with Section 14 of the said Act."

— Kerala High Court, July 15 Order

Kerala Advocate General Jaju Babu conceded during the hearing that there were "infirmities" in the Board's constitution. In a state affidavit filed on July 14, the government acknowledged the need to reconstitute the Board in compliance with the law. Senior Advocate T. Krishnanunni, representing the Board, admitted that two non-Muslim members had not been nominated, attributing the delay to pending Supreme Court proceedings — a claim both the Additional Solicitor General and the petitioners disputed, noting no such cases were pending.

Political Fallout in Kerala

The court battle has triggered sharp political exchanges in Kerala. A Congress MLA accused the ruling CPM of "spreading false propaganda" about the Waqf Board case, alleging the party was misleading the Muslim community about the implications of the 2025 amendment. The BJP, which filed the lead PIL through Shone George, has demanded strict enforcement of the non-Muslim member requirement, framing it as a matter of statutory compliance rather than communal politics.

The Kerala government, led by the CPM-headed Left Democratic Front until the 2026 assembly elections brought the Congress-led United Democratic Front to power, had nominated all nine members as Muslims through a February 2026 government order — with a promise to appoint the remaining two non-Muslim members "shortly" that was never fulfilled.

Fresh Challenge: Shia Representation

Adding another layer to the dispute, a Shia Muslim group has separately moved the Kerala High Court seeking representation on the Board. The 2025 Waqf Amendment Act requires representation from Shia, Sunni, Bohra, and Aghakhani communities. The ACTS petition before the High Court had already flagged the absence of Shia members, and the court's July 15 order noted this deficiency alongside the missing non-Muslim members.

Broader Waqf Amendment Battle

The Kerala dispute unfolds against the backdrop of a nationwide legal battle over the Waqf (Amendment) Act, 2025, which came into force on April 8, 2025. The Supreme Court is separately hearing petitions challenging the constitutional validity of the amendment, which introduced sweeping changes including mandatory non-Muslim membership on Waqf Boards, new provisions on de-notifying Waqf properties, and enhanced government oversight.

The 2025 amendment was enacted after receiving what the Centre described as "lakhs of representations" from citizens concerned about Waqf Board overreach, particularly in cases like the Munambam land dispute in Kerala where the Board's unilateral declaration of over 400 acres as Waqf property affected hundreds of Hindu and Christian families.

What Comes Next

With the Supreme Court removing the government supervision requirement, the Kerala Waqf Board is no longer under a bureaucratic overseer — but it remains constrained from taking major decisions without High Court permission. The underlying composition challenge before the Kerala High Court is expected to be heard within two weeks, during which the state government may move to reconstitute the Board with the mandatory non-Muslim and Shia members. The Supreme Court's intervention underscores the sensitivity of the Waqf governance issue and the delicate balance courts are trying to maintain between statutory compliance and institutional autonomy.
